       1             SENATOR FLANAGAN:  And, a couple of very

       3             Actually, why don't we stand, and I'm going

       7        hearing recite, as follows:)

       8             "I pledge allegiance to the flag of the

      11      with liberty and justice for all."

      12             SENATOR FLANAGAN:  Thank you.

      13             And today, everyone in this room pays

      14      attention, so we are all acutely aware of what

      15      happened a year ago.

      16             I would respectfully ask for a moment of

      17      silence for all the people who suffered last year,

      18      and, frankly, people who are still suffering as we

      21             SENATOR FLANAGAN:  Thank you very much.

      24      attended one of the other hearings as well, up in

      25      Syracuse;





 

                                                                  6
       1             Senator Felder, who is co-chairing this

       2      hearing, and is the Chair of the New York City

       3      Subcommittee on Education;

       4             Senator Betty Little;

       5             And, of course, Senator Marty Golden, who has

       6      just arrived.

       7             This room is a little different than some of

       8      the other rooms we've worked in, and I appreciate

       9      everyone's patience, among other things.

      10             We are going to do a couple of very basic

      11      things.

      12             For anyone who has paid attention to the

      13      other hearings that we've had, we started in

      14      Long Island, went to Syracuse, went to Buffalo.

      15             We are now, obviously, in the city of

      16      New York, and have a hearing the 13th of November in

      17      Albany.  That will to be fifth and final hearing.

      18             As we have previously mentioned, we will be

      19      taking in all testimony.

      20             Anyone who sends in e-mails or letters or

      21      anything like that, it will all be made part of the

      22      public record, and that will be closed out,

      23      effective November 15th.

      24             So if you want to put anything in after the

      25      last hearing, feel free to do it, and we do know





 

                                                                  7
       1      that people are watching and listening, and we have

       2      gotten hundreds of e-mails.

       3             We've endeavored to put everything online as

       4      quickly as possible.

       5             The testimony that's in today should be up

       6      online already.

       7             And just in terms of format, I will do this

       8      as politely and diplomatically as possible:

       9             Nobody is going to read their testimony.

      10             Everyone's competent to read on their own and

      11      individually.

      15             We have a lot of diverse people joining us

      16      today, and I think it underscores what we try to do

      17      at these hearings; and that is, actually get public

      18      input.

      19             I will take credit, along with my colleagues,

      20      we started having these hearings and announced them

      21      long before anyone was doing any kind of public

      22      forums, and these are formal public hearings of the

      23      Senate Education Committee.

      25      people are going to have very cogent, succinct, and

       1      comments that are on target.

       2             Oh, I'm sorry.

       3             We've been joined by Senator Hoylman.

       4             And our first person who will be testifying

       5      is the Chancellor, and I know I can't really see her

       6      because of the pole right in the middle of the room

       7      here, but, Chancellor Tisch, would you join us?

       8             CHANCELLOR MERRYL TISCH:  Good morning,

       9      everyone.

      10             It's really a pleasure to be here this

      11      morning.

      12             I am deeply aware that I sit before you, and

      13      sit with you, during a remarkably complicated time

      14      in the history of education and educational reform

      15      in this country, and, for our particular purposes,

      16      in the state of New York today.

      17             As everyone in this room I think is acutely

      18      aware, the Regents Reform Agenda, which is being led

      19      by our very able Commissioner John King, is a

      20      complicated conversation about raising standards for

      21      all of New York; that means our entire state.

      22             We are acutely aware that we are facing

      23      enormous challenges as we have moved from the

      24      twentieth century to the twenty-first century.

      25             We are very aware of the fact that, as we





 

                                                                  9
       1      look at some of the indicators for success in a

       2      system in which we spend $54 billion a year

       3      statewide, it is incumbent upon us to consistently

       4      question what we are doing, what our practices are,

       5      what we need to change, what we need to modify.

       6             In 2010, the State Education Department

       7      decided that it was time to look at our graduation

       8      rates, and what they really meant in terms of

       9      students' ability to attain a -- what I believe is a

      10      ticket to the future, which every child in this

      11      state is entitled to by virtue of their citizenship

      12      in the greatest state in this country.

      13             And what we learned, that even though we were

      14      reporting graduation rates that were 74 percent

      15      statewide, when we looked at the remediation rates

      16      that students were having in our two-year colleges,

      17      we noticed that, in fact, statewide, 50 percent of

      18      the students going on to two-year colleges needed to

      19      be remediated.

      20             That means that the taxpayers of

      21      New York State were paying college tuition for

      22      academic achievement that should have been put to

      23      bed in high school.

      24             In New York City, when we look at the

      25      achievement rate by college- and career-ready, we





 

                                                                  10
       1      look at a rate that says 22 percent.

       2             When we look at our special-education

       3      students across this state, we see that very few of

       4      them go on to have a future.

       5             When we look at our English-language

       6      learners, we see very few of them go on to graduate

       7      high school in a way that prepares them to be part

       8      of a twenty-first-century economy.

       9             The Obama Administration embarked upon

      10      something that was called Race to the Top.

      11             Now, we can agree with the challenge grant or

      12      we can disagree with the challenge grant, but

      13      New York State knew what was coming down the

      14      pipeline.

      15             We knew that the attainment of Common Core

      16      Standards, which was the next level of standards,

      17      was going to be a critical part of what was going to

      18      take place in terms of educational reform in this

      19      country during the eight years of this

      20      administration.

      21             There were two ways to go:  New York State

      22      could compete and get resources to help us implement

      23      Race to the Top reforms and common Core Adjustment,

      24      or we could not compete.

      25             We decided to compete, and we won a





 

                                                                  11
       1      $700 million grant to this state.

       2             I would like you all to note that 45 states

       3      have adopted Common Core.  Only 11 of them have

       4      received Race to the Top dollars.

       5             Our decision was simple:  Should we take

       6      money from the federal government to help us

       7      implement a reform that was going to be part of a

       8      national conversation, and actually help our cities

       9      and our municipalities with this adjustment, or,

      10      should we not?

      11             I think it made sense for us to compete for

      12      these dollars and to use them appropriately.

      13             Our reform was not only the adoption of

      14      Common Core standards, but it was a very, very

      15      serious look and challenge to our schools of

      16      education and the preparation of our teachers.

      17             We have put forth, I think, a very cogent

      18      reform.

      19             We are in the middle of implementation.

      20             Yes, New York is leading the charge

      21      nationally, and what we have gone through in this

      22      past year as we've outlaid our Common Core tests,

      23      I am the first to admit, has created a lot of

      24      upheaval and displacement, but, we have also taken

      25      very important steps to assure that our students and





 

                                                                  12
       1      our parents and our teachers can be part of this

       2      conversation.

       3             We applied for a waiver to the federal

       4      government which said, since New York State is going

       5      ahead and implementing Common Core testing, could

       6      we, in fact, not identify anymore schools or school

       7      districts for failure based on the first year of

       8      implementation?

       9             We got that waiver.

      10             We are now going to be applying for a waiver

      11      to the federal government to allow us some relief

      12      when it comes to the testing of English-language

      13      learners and special-education students.

      14             We do not believe that the federal guidelines

      15      which require students with special needs to be

      16      tested at age level rather than competency level is

      17      a way to conduct great policy.

      18             We will be forcefully pushing for these

      19      waivers.

      20             We are going to be forcefully asking for

      21      many, many types of federal relief to allow this

      22      implementation to take hold.

      23             But, I don't kid myself.

      24             I think that what we have put forward

      25      requires a lot of conversation, and a lot of ability





 

                                                                  13
       1      to listen, to adjust, to be thoughtful, to be

       2      transparent, but I believe we are embarking on a

       3      generational change, and generational changes often

       4      cause upheaval.

       5             It is never our intent to impose.

       6             It is our intent to use public policy as a

       7      critical tool to help our students, parents, and

       8      teachers partake in a twenty-first century economy.

       9             Thank you very much for this opportunity to

      10      be with you here today.

      12      on, I just want to recognize, Assemblywoman Schimel

      13      has joined us, she is sitting in the audience.  She

      14      is a passionate educational person.

      15             And we've also have been joined by

      16      Senator Toby Stavisky.

      17             Toby, welcome.

      18             And I also just want to let everybody know,

      19      when these things go well, you know it never happens

      20      in isolation.

      21             So, we have really good support staff.  All

      22      the ability to see this and hear it and record it

      23      properly, these gentlemen, who spent probably more

      24      time traveling in their cars than anybody all over

      25      the state, are very helpful to all of us.





 

                                                                  14
       1             So, want to thank them.

       2             And, any of my colleagues have questions?

       3             Senator Little?

       4             SENATOR LITTLE:  Yes.

       5             Thank you very much, and thank you for your

       6      comments.

       7             I just want to note, I was really pleased to

       8      see that the Regents is looking at substituting some

       9      tests, and removing.

      10             I mean, New York State has always been known

      11      for their, you know, really rigid testing program

      12      and standardization among our schools, but when

      13      we've added all these other tests, I think it is so

      14      overdone, and it's really difficult.

      15             And as a teacher myself, and I would say,

      16      even though I'm from way up north, I did have a

      17      New York City permanent certification to teach

      18      elementary school, which I'm sure has expired a long

      19      time ago; but, nevertheless, I did teach in

      20      Staten Island.

      21             So -- but I think it's something that we have

      22      to look at, and I also believe -- I mentioned this

      23      at the other one -- that the results of these tests

      24      need to come back to the teachers; not just an

      25      analysis, but the actual results of the tests, so





 

                                                                  15
       1      the teacher who is working with these children now

       2      knows who got it, who didn't; what she might be

       3      doing wrong or he might be doing wrong in their

       4      presentation; and how to reach out to these children

       5      better.

       6             If we really want the children to benefit

       7      from the tests, rather than just collect data,

       8      I think we have to do more than just give a general

       9      analysis of these tests back to the teachers, so

      10      that they see can just how each child understood

      11      what has been taught.

      12             CHANCELLOR MERRYL TISCH:  We are very mindful

      13      of the ability to use tests really for their

      14      purpose, which is to inform instruction.

      15             I would say that I think, this year, we

      16      published 25 to 30 percent of the testing items.

      17             The issue that we have to always keep in the

      18      back of our mind is the costs of putting all those

      19      items out there, and then having to do a whole new

      20      test every year, and the amount of time that would

      21      be required to field-test all of the new items.

      22             So what we need to do is find the right

      23      balance.

      24             As we go forward, I am sure that we will

      25      achieve the right balance, and, we are very





 

                                                                  16
       1      cognizant of that.

       2             SENATOR LITTLE:  But just as an example, we

       3      had -- I represent 48 school districts, and one of

       4      my teachers, and I heard this from the

       5      superintendent, he had to put a violation in her

       6      personal record because she took notes on the test,

       7      and, you know, kind of made some notes to herself as

       8      to things that were being asked, and how it was

       9      being presented to the children.

      10             And that just seems wrong.

      11             CHANCELLOR MERRYL TISCH:  I couldn't agree

      12      with you more.

      13             I think, you know, public policy, as I said

      14      before, has to be a living and breathing thing.

      15             And when we are made aware of these things,

      16      it is our -- I think it is incumbent upon us to

      17      adjust them.

      18             But I want to also be clear, that along the

      19      way to adjusting, we can't allow ourselves to be put

      20      into a place where we fall back on old practice that

      21      doesn't serve us well.

      22             So I would say, Senator, yes, we should pay

      23      attention to all of these things that you all hear

      24      every day in your districts, because that's the

      25      right thing to do.





 

                                                                  17
       1             But it is also the right thing for us, as we

       2      adjust, to be mindful of the larger goals; and, so,

       3      it's the balance.

       4             SENATOR LITTLE:  Thank you.

       5             SENATOR FLANAGAN:  Senator Hoylman.

       6             SENATOR HOYLMAN:  Thank you.

       7             And thank you for holding this important

       8      hearing here in Manhattan.

       9             And thank you, Madam Chancellor, for being

      10      here today, and thank you for your leadership over

      11      the years; it's greatly appreciated.

      12             I represent part of Manhattan, and --

      13             CHANCELLOR MERRYL TISCH:  We like Manhattan.

      14             SENATOR HOYLMAN:  Yes.

      15             And there is a-- I'm in touch with a number

      16      of public-school parents across my district.

      17             I have a 2-year-old myself, she's not yet in

      18      school.

      19             But as I think you know, there's tremendous

      20      anxiety among parents and children.

      21             CHANCELLOR MERRYL TISCH:  I'm kind of anxious

      22      myself, so, believe me, I'm paying attention to all

      23      the anxiety.

      24             SENATOR HOYLMAN:  And, uhm, for starters, you

      25      know, the more information I think parents can learn





 

                                                                  18
       1      about the Common Core, the better, so forums like

       2      this I think are important.

       3             The Commissioner has engaged in a number of

       4      public forums across the state.

       5             I just wanted to point out that I'm

       6      disappointed; in the first round, he has not chosen

       7      to have a forum in New York City.

       8             CHANCELLOR MERRYL TISCH:  So let me --

       9                  [Applause.]

      10             CHANCELLOR MERRYL TISCH:  I appreciate that.

      11             Let me just say that the forums that have

      12      been announced were really the forums that were

      13      outside of New York City.  And within the next week

      14      or so we will be announcing three or four forums

      18      there could be more.

       6             SENATOR HOYLMAN:  If I could ask one more

       7      question, which is about data and privacy, which

       8      I know you hear a lot of.

       9             Can you give us any update on your efforts to

      12             As you probably can expect, I have many

      15      test companies.

      16             CHANCELLOR MERRYL TISCH:  You know, I would

      17      like Ira Schwartz from the department to answer

      18      that.

      19             These are really technical questions that

      20      I think really deserve very thoughtful responses.

      21             Don't screw up.

      22                  [Laughter.]

      23             IRA SCHWARTZ:  Good morning.

      24             As we have indicated, New York has had, and

      25      has been rolling out, a system for a number of





 

                                                                  20
       1      years, where we -- students have unique student

       2      IDs that are used for us to gather information

       3      about assessment results and other critical

       4      information.

       5             It is not based on social security numbers or

       6      anything of that nature.

       7             Every school district currently has many,

       8      many contracts with third-party vendors to collect

       9      information for a variety of purposes.

      10             They collect information because of bus

      11      routes or school lunch, for assessments, for

      12      scheduling; for many, many purposes.

      13             The system that we are putting in place is

      14      simply designed to make it easier for all of that

      15      information to be collected together and used, and

      16      it is -- it does not in any way change the ability

      17      of that information to be used outside of the

      18      agreements that are already in place between a

      19      school district and that vendor, and confidentiality

      20      of all of that information must be maintained.

      21             So this is -- what we have been talking about

      22      is simply a better way to be able to take

      23      information that is already collected, to work with

      24      vendors who are already under contract by school

      25      districts, so that, for example, if you are an





 

                                                                  21
       1      administrator in a school district, you don't have

       2      to deal with having 17 different passwords and

       3      17 different systems that you have to go through.

       4             It is simply a way of collecting this

       5      information and using it with more efficiency; not

       6      in any way to make it available to others that are

       7      not able to access it now.

       8             SENATOR HOYLMAN:  So private student data

       9      will not be sold to third parties--

      10             IRA SCHWARTZ:  No, it will not.

      11             SENATOR HOYLMAN:  -- or provided to

      12      third-party vendors?

      13             IRA SCHWARTZ:  It will be provided only under

      14      the contracts that already exist.  It is not going

      17      that this is like, you know, you go onto a website,

      18      and because you've gone onto that website, all of a

      19      sudden, you're going to start getting e-mails from

      20      somebody who you have never had a relationship with.

      21             The security, the privacy, of all of this

      22      information remains under the same constraints that

      23      districts are currently working with their providers

      24      of various services for.

      25             SENATOR FLANAGAN:  Senator Tkaczyk, and then





 

                                                                  22
       1      Senator Stavisky.

       2             SENATOR TKACZYK:  Just to follow up on that,

       3      what specific information is provided to outside

       4      vendors?

       6      relationship is with the vendor and what the purpose

      15      parent -- parent of a special-needs child and I'm

      16      concerned about my child's condition being shared

      17      with outside vendors, is that a cause for concern?

      18             IRA SCHWARTZ:  I do not believe it is a cause

      19      for concern.

      21      all, thank you for holding this hearing and for

      22      being here today in New York City.

      25      a chance to implement the Common Core curriculum,
